facts.claim: Complexity: Stage I: max probing depth 4 mm or less, mostly horizontal bone loss. Stage II: max probing depth 5 mm or less, mostly horizontal bone loss. facts.claim: Step 2 (cause-related therapy) is subgingival instrumentation to remove subgingival biofilm and calculus. Hand or powered (sonic/ultrasonic) instruments, alone or combined, are both recommended, and it may be done quadrant by quadrant or as full-mouth delivery within 24 hours.

facts.claim: Tooth-prognosis systems weigh tooth-level factors, and some also weigh patient-level factors. The conventional categories are good, fair, poor, questionable and hopeless. McGuire and Nunn (1996) assign prognosis from clinical attachment level, furcation involvement, mobility, crown-to-root ratio and root form, without patient factors. Kwok and Caton (2007) assign one of four categories and add general (patient) factors such as compliance, plaque control, smoking and diabetes to local factors such as probing depth, attachment loss, plaque-retentive anatomy, trauma from occlusion and habits, and mobility.
facts.conditions: The quotes do not name Kwok and Caton's four categories, so don't key their category names. The quote listing good/fair/poor/questionable/hopeless calls them the conventional categories without naming a system. Sources: two open-access J Clin Periodontol/Clin Oral Investig studies describing the systems, not the original 1996/2007 papers.

facts.claim: Prognosis systems are better at predicting which teeth will be kept than which will be lost. In a 5-year cohort in supportive periodontal care, teeth in the worst category were lost 14 to 77 times as often as teeth in the best category, yet most teeth labeled hopeless were still retained: specificity and negative predictive value were good, sensitivity and positive predictive value low. Older studies found that a hopeless prognosis wrongly predicted loss in 19.6% to 38% of cases and a questionable prognosis in 37% to 74%, while a prediction that a tooth would not be lost failed only 0.46% to 2% of the time.
facts.conditions: Cohort of compliant maintenance patients (97 patients, UK practice) with few teeth in the worst categories; teach the direction (good specificity, low sensitivity: many hopeless teeth survive with maintenance), not the exact multipliers.

facts.claim: Tooth-level factors that predict tooth loss in treated periodontitis patients: bone loss, furcation involvement, probing depth, mobility, tooth type, crown-to-root ratio, and use of the tooth as an abutment. In a 10-year maintenance cohort, abutment function, diabetes, bone loss, furcation involvement and age predicted tooth loss. Even teeth with very advanced bone loss (over 75%) have been kept for 10 years or more.

facts.claim: Patient-level factors that worsen tooth prognosis: a systematic review (cited by a 2018 prediction-model study) found older age and smoking to be the only patient factors clearly associated with tooth loss from periodontitis during maintenance, and diabetes predicted tooth loss in a 10-year maintenance cohort. A 2018 prediction model also used heavy smoking, bruxism, severe periodontitis and the baseline number of teeth as patient-related predictors; its authors suggest the combined impact of smoking and bruxism may matter more than previously suspected.

facts.claim: EFP S3 guideline (R3.10, grade A): molars with Class II or III furcation involvement and residual pockets should receive periodontal therapy, and furcation involvement is no reason for extraction. For mandibular molars with residual pockets and Class II furcation involvement, periodontal regenerative surgery is recommended (R3.11).

facts.claim: Tooth prognosis is not fixed. Teeth can move between categories as periodontal and restorative status changes (attachment or bone gain, less mobility or furcation involvement), and patient factors such as motivation, stress or diabetes control can change during maintenance. A questionable tooth in a motivated patient with a good overall prognosis can do better than the same tooth in a noncompliant patient with other risk factors. Non-periodontal factors also decide survival: in one 5-year cohort, only 9 of 31 extracted teeth were lost for periodontal reasons (others: fracture, caries, endodontic pathology), so restorability and endodontic status belong in the prognosis.
facts.conditions: The 9-of-31 figure comes from one cohort of compliant patients in supportive care; teach the principle, not the number.
